title: Inequality and Social Mobility
bigQuestion: How much does the place and family you are born into shape the life you can build?

story.title: Two Babies, One Birthday
story.kicker: A student follows two newborns, one in Oslo and one in São Paulo, and asks what their chances really are.
paragraphs: Mariana is in tenth grade, and her project starts with a simple idea. Picture two babies born on the same morning. One is born in a hospital in Oslo, the capital of Norway. The other is born in a hospital in São Paulo, the largest city in Brazil. Both are healthy. Both have parents who love them. Mariana wants to know what the numbers say about the lives ahead of them.

She starts with money. Norway is one of the most equal countries in the world, measured by how income is shared. Brazil is one of the most unequal. In São Paulo, glass towers with rooftop helicopter pads stand a short drive from crowded hillside neighborhoods called favelas. In Oslo, the gap between a bus driver's pay and a lawyer's pay is smaller than in most countries.

Next she looks at schools and health. Both babies can go to free public schools. But in Brazil, many families who can afford it pay for private schools, and the public schools vary a great deal. In Norway, almost every child goes to the same kind of public school. Mariana notices that the Oslo baby's future seems to depend less on which family she was born into.

Then Mariana finds a surprise. Some economists argue that countries with bigger gaps between rich and poor also have less movement between generations. In those places, children tend to stay near where their parents started. Other economists question how strong that link is. Mariana realizes her project is really about one question: how much of a life is set at birth, and how much can a person change?
story.think: What would you want to know about a country to guess how much a baby born there could move up in life?

lessons.title: Income Versus Wealth
lessons.mainIdea: Income is money coming in over time, while wealth is what a person owns minus what they owe, and wealth is usually far more unequal.
reading: Think about two neighbors. Ana earns $80,000 a year as a nurse, but she rents her apartment and still owes money on student loans. Ben earns $40,000 a year at a part-time job, but he inherited a paid-off house and some savings from his grandparents. Who is better off? The answer depends on whether you look at income or wealth.

*Income* is the money that comes in over a period of time, such as wages, salary, rent from property, or interest from savings. *Wealth* is a snapshot of everything a person owns, such as a home, savings and stocks, minus everything they owe. Economists call wealth *net worth*. A person can have a high income but little wealth, or a small income but a lot of wealth.

The difference matters because wealth is usually shared much less evenly than income. In the United States, the Federal Reserve estimates that the richest tenth of households hold about two-thirds of all household wealth. The bottom half of households hold only a few percent. Wealth can also be passed down to children, so it helps explain why advantages can last across generations.

Wealth also acts as a cushion. A family with savings can survive a lost job or a medical bill. A family with no savings may have to borrow at high interest. Wealth can pay for college, a first home, or starting a business. That is why many researchers who study opportunity look closely at wealth, not just at paychecks.

words.d: money that comes in over a period of time, such as wages, salary or interest
the total value of what a person or family owns, minus what they owe
another name for wealth: assets minus debts

look.title: Who Holds U.S. Household Wealth
look.cite: Federal Reserve Board, Distributional Financial Accounts, estimates for about 2023 (rounded)
look.prompt: The bottom half of households is 50 percent of people. About what share of wealth does it hold, and what does that gap tell you?

check.q: Which of these is an example of wealth rather than income?
check.why: Wealth is what a person owns minus debts. A house is owned property, while paychecks, salary and tips are income.

check.q: In the reading, why might Ben be better off than Ana in some ways?
choices: Ben owns an inherited house and savings
check.why: Ben earns less income, but he has more wealth because he inherited a paid-off house and savings.

check.q: According to the Federal Reserve estimate in the reading, the richest tenth of U.S. households hold about what share of wealth?
check.why: The reading says the richest tenth hold about two-thirds of household wealth, which shows how unequal wealth is.

lessons.title: The Gini Coefficient
lessons.mainIdea: The Gini coefficient is one number, from 0 to 1, that sums up how evenly income is shared in a country.
reading: Imagine a class of 30 students sharing 30 pizzas. If every student gets one pizza, the sharing is perfectly equal. If one student gets all 30 and everyone else gets nothing, the sharing is perfectly unequal. Real countries fall somewhere in between. Economists wanted one simple number to show where a country falls on that scale.

The most common tool is the *Gini coefficient*, named after the Italian statistician Corrado Gini, who described it in 1912. It runs from 0 to 1. A score of 0 means everyone has the same income. A score of 1 means one person has all of it. Many reports multiply the score by 100, so a Gini of 0.40 is often written as 40. Higher means more *inequality*, or a bigger gap.

The World Bank publishes Gini estimates for most countries. Nordic countries such as Norway, Denmark and Finland usually score in the mid to high 20s. The United States scores around 40. Latin America is often described as one of the most unequal regions, with Brazil and Colombia scoring above 50. South Africa has one of the highest scores measured anywhere, above 60.

A single number has limits. Two countries can have the same Gini but very different lives at the bottom. The Gini also says nothing about why a gap exists. Some measures use income before taxes, and others use income after taxes and government benefits. So careful readers always ask: which income, which year, and measured by whom?

words.d: a number from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has everything) that measures how evenly income is shared
a gap in how income, wealth or opportunity is shared among people
an expert who collects and studies numbers to find patterns

look.title: Income Gaps Around the World
look.cite: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform, recent estimates (rounded; years differ by country)
look.prompt: Which country on this list has the most equal income sharing, and which has the least? How can you tell?

check.q: A country's Gini coefficient rises from 0.30 to 0.45. What does that mean?
check.why: A higher Gini means a bigger gap in how income is shared. It does not measure total wealth or population.

check.q: Which region does the reading describe as one of the most unequal in the world?
check.why: The reading says Latin America is often described as one of the most unequal regions, with Brazil and Colombia above 50.

check.q: What is one limit of the Gini coefficient named in the reading?
choices: It only works for Nordic countries
It does not explain why a gap exists
It cannot be written as a number
check.why: The reading says the Gini sums up the gap in one number but says nothing about its causes.

lessons.title: Poverty Lines and Living Standards
lessons.mainIdea: Poverty can be measured against a fixed line, like the World Bank's line for extreme poverty, or against what is normal in one country.
reading: A family in rural Malawi and a family in Chicago may both be called poor. Yet their lives are very different. The Malawi family may lack clean water and electricity. The Chicago family may have both but struggle to pay rent. To compare them, researchers need clear rules about what counts as poverty.

One rule is *absolute poverty*, which uses a fixed line that does not change from country to country. The World Bank sets an international line for *extreme poverty*. In 2022 it set that line at $2.15 per person per day, adjusted for prices in each country. In 2025 it raised the line to $3.00, using newer price data. Below that line, people struggle to afford enough food, shelter and basic care.

Another rule is *relative poverty*. Here, a person is poor if they have much less than most people in their own country. Many European countries count a household as poor if its income is below 60 percent of the middle income. Under this rule, a family in Norway could count as poor even though it lives far above the World Bank line.

Each measure answers a different question. Absolute lines ask whether people can meet basic needs. Relative lines ask whether people can take part in normal life where they live, like joining a school trip. Arguments about poverty often come down to which measure a speaker is using, so it helps to ask.

words.d: being below a fixed income line needed for basic needs, the same in every country
the World Bank's term for living below its lowest international poverty line
having much less income than most people in your own country

look.title: Two Kinds of Poor
look.text: Family A lives in a village with no electricity. The parents grow most of their own food, and in dry years the children eat once a day. Family B lives in a city apartment with heat and a phone. But after rent, there is little money for school clothes, and the children skip class trips because they cost too much.
look.prompt: Which family is in absolute poverty, and which fits relative poverty better? Explain using the terms.

check.q: Which measure would call a family poor because it earns much less than most families in its own country?
check.why: Relative poverty compares a family to others in the same country, such as below 60 percent of the middle income.

check.q: In 2022 the World Bank set its extreme poverty line at about how much per person per day?
check.why: The reading gives the World Bank's 2022 international extreme poverty line as $2.15 per person per day, adjusted for prices.

check.q: Why can a family in Norway count as poor under one measure but not another?
choices: It may be below Norway's relative line but far above the World Bank line
The World Bank does not measure Europe
check.why: Relative poverty compares to others in Norway, while the World Bank's absolute line is a fixed amount.

lessons.title: What Social Mobility Means
lessons.mainIdea: Social mobility is how easily people move up or down the ladder of income and status, especially compared with their parents.
reading: Picture a ladder with ten rungs. Everyone in a country stands on one rung, from the lowest incomes to the highest. Now picture the children of each person. Do the children end up on the same rung as their parents? Or do some climb higher and some slip lower? That movement is what *social mobility* means.

Researchers study two kinds. *Intergenerational mobility* compares children with their parents, such as a farmworker's daughter who becomes an engineer. Movement within one person's lifetime is called intra-generational mobility, like a cashier who becomes a store manager. Mobility can also be *absolute* or relative. Absolute mobility asks whether children earn more than their parents did at the same age. Relative mobility asks whether children change rungs compared with everyone else.

The economist Raj Chetty and his team studied tax records to measure absolute mobility in the United States. They found that about 90 percent of Americans born in 1940 grew up to earn more than their parents. For those born in 1980, it was about 50 percent. Slower economic growth and wider gaps both played a part, they argued.

High mobility is often seen as a sign of fairness. It suggests that talent and effort, not just family, shape where people end up. But people disagree about how much mobility is realistic and what helps it most. Some point to schools and neighborhoods. Others point to families, work and a growing economy.

words.d: movement of people up or down the ladder of income, education or status
how much children's position differs from their parents' position
whether children end up earning more than their parents did at the same age

look.title: Earning More Than Your Parents
look.cite: Chetty and others, "The Fading American Dream," Science, 2017 (rounded)
look.prompt: How did the chance of out-earning your parents change from 1940 to 1980? What might explain the drop?

check.q: A farmworker's daughter becomes an engineer. What kind of mobility is this?
check.why: Intergenerational mobility compares a child's position with her parents' position.

check.q: According to Chetty's research, about what share of Americans born in 1980 out-earned their parents?
check.why: The study found about 90 percent for those born in 1940 but only about 50 percent for those born in 1980.

check.q: What question does absolute mobility ask?
choices: Do children earn more than their parents did at the same age?
Do children change rungs compared with everyone else?
How equal is income in a country?
How much wealth does a family own?
check.why: Absolute mobility compares a child's earnings with the parents' earnings at the same age.

lessons.title: The Great Gatsby Curve
lessons.mainIdea: Economists describe a pattern called the Great Gatsby curve: countries with more inequality tend to have less mobility between generations.
reading: In the novel The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, a poor young man remakes himself as a rich one. But he never fully breaks into the old-money world he admires. In 2012 the economist Alan Krueger, then an adviser to the U.S. president, borrowed the book's title for a graph. The graph used research by the Canadian economist Miles Corak.

The graph places countries on two measures. One is income inequality, often measured by the Gini coefficient. The other is how closely children's earnings follow their parents' earnings. Economists call that second measure *earnings persistence*. When they drew the dots, a pattern appeared. Countries like Denmark and Norway had low inequality and low persistence. The United States and the United Kingdom had higher inequality and higher persistence.

This pattern is called the *Great Gatsby curve*. It is a *correlation*, meaning two things rise and fall together. A correlation does not prove that one causes the other. Supporters argue that big gaps let rich families buy advantages, such as better schools and tutors, which keeps children near their parents' rung.

Critics raise questions. Some say the countries differ in many ways, such as size, history and population, so the curve may mix up causes. Others say the data for some countries are weak. Still others argue that growth and strong families matter more than gaps. Economists still debate how much the curve tells us about cause.

words.d: a graph showing that countries with more income inequality tend to have less mobility between generations
a pattern where two things tend to change together, which does not by itself prove cause
how closely children's earnings follow their parents' earnings

look.title: Reading the Curve
look.text: Imagine a graph. Across the bottom is inequality, from low on the left to high on the right. Up the side is how much parents' earnings predict their children's earnings. Denmark and Norway sit near the lower left. The United States and the United Kingdom sit toward the upper right. Most other countries fall along a rising line between them.
look.prompt: What does the rising line suggest? Name one reason the line alone cannot prove that inequality causes low mobility.

check.q: Who named the Great Gatsby curve in 2012?
check.why: Alan Krueger named the curve in 2012, using research by Miles Corak.

check.q: Where do Denmark and Norway fall on the curve?
choices: Low inequality and low earnings persistence
High inequality and high earnings persistence
High inequality and low earnings persistence
check.why: The reading says the Nordic countries have low inequality, and children's earnings follow their parents' less closely.

check.q: Why do critics say the curve does not prove cause?
choices: It is a correlation, and countries differ in many other ways
check.why: A correlation shows two things moving together. Other differences between countries could explain the pattern.

lessons.title: Education as a Ladder
lessons.mainIdea: Education is one of the strongest ladders for moving up, but unequal schools can also pass advantages down.
reading: In 1862 President Abraham Lincoln signed the Morrill Act. It gave federal land to states to build public colleges. The University of Illinois grew from that law. For millions of students since then, a public college has been a step up. Education is often called a ladder because it can lift people whose parents never had the chance.

The numbers show why. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that workers with a bachelor's degree earn much more, on average, than workers with only a high school diploma. They are also less likely to be out of work. Economists call the extra pay for a degree the *college premium*. Skills and training are sometimes called *human capital*, because they work like an investment that pays off later.

But the ladder is not equal for everyone. In the United States, schools are partly paid for by local property taxes. Richer areas can often spend more per student. Families with more money can pay for tutors, test preparation and summer programs. So schooling can lift some students up while helping others stay ahead.

Countries try different fixes. Finland gives every school similar funding and trains all teachers to a high level. South Korea has intense exams, and many families pay for private after-school academies called hagwons. People argue about which approach helps most. Many agree that early childhood learning and strong teachers make a real difference.

words.d: the extra pay, on average, that workers with a college degree earn compared with those without one
the skills, knowledge and training a person has that help them earn a living
an 1862 U.S. law that gave land to states to build public colleges

look.title: What a Diploma Pays
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, "Education pays," 2023 data (rounded)
look.prompt: About how much more per week does the typical worker with a bachelor's degree earn than one with a high school diploma?

check.q: What is the college premium?
choices: The extra average pay earned by workers with a degree
check.why: The college premium is the extra pay, on average, that degree holders earn compared with people without one.

check.q: How can U.S. schooling keep some advantages in place, according to the reading?
choices: All schools get the same money
Richer areas can spend more, and families can pay for tutors
The Morrill Act closed public colleges
check.why: Local property taxes and private spending on tutoring can give richer students extra help.

check.q: Which country is described as giving every school similar funding?
check.why: The reading says Finland gives schools similar funding and trains all teachers to a high level.

lessons.title: Class in Britain
lessons.mainIdea: In the United Kingdom, class has long been signaled by accent and schooling, and a small group from private schools still holds many top jobs.
reading: In Britain, people have often been able to guess each other's class within a few words. For generations, an accent called *Received Pronunciation* was linked to the upper and upper-middle class and to the BBC. Regional accents from Liverpool, Glasgow or East London were sometimes looked down on. Many working-class Britons are proud of their accents, and today the BBC hires presenters with many different ones.

Schools are another signal. In Britain, the oldest private schools, such as Eton and Harrow, are confusingly called public schools. Fees are high. The Sutton Trust, a charity that studies mobility, reports that only about 7 percent of British pupils attend private schools. Yet its 2019 study found that people from private schools held a much larger share of top jobs, such as senior judges.

The word *elite* means a small group at the top of a society. Critics argue that Britain's elite reproduces itself, with the same schools feeding the same universities, Oxford and Cambridge, and then the same jobs. Supporters of private schools reply that parents have a right to choose, and that the schools often give scholarships and share facilities.

Britain has also changed a great deal. After World War II, free secondary school and later new universities opened doors. Many prime ministers since then went to state schools. The debate today is about how fast the doors are opening, and what would open them wider.

words.d: a British accent long linked with the upper classes, schools like Eton and early BBC radio
a small group at the top of a society in wealth, power or status
in Britain, an old private fee-paying school such as Eton; in the U.S., a free government school

look.title: Private School and Top Jobs in Britain
look.cite: Sutton Trust and Social Mobility Commission, Elitist Britain, 2019 (rounded)
look.prompt: Compare the first row with the others. What pattern do you see, and what are two possible explanations?

check.q: In Britain, what does the term public school usually mean?
choices: A school run by the BBC
check.why: In Britain, old fee-paying schools like Eton are called public schools, unlike the American meaning.

check.q: According to the Sutton Trust, about what share of British pupils attend private schools?
check.why: The reading says only about 7 percent attend private schools, yet they hold a larger share of top jobs.

check.q: What argument do supporters of private schools make?
choices: Parents have a right to choose, and schools offer scholarships
Private schools should replace all state schools
check.why: The reading says supporters stress parents' choice and point to scholarships and shared facilities.

lessons.title: India's Reservations Debate
lessons.mainIdea: India reserves places in colleges, government jobs and legislatures for groups that faced caste discrimination, and people still debate how the system should work.
reading: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was born in 1891 into a caste that others treated as untouchable. As a boy, he was made to sit apart at school. He went on to earn doctorates in New York and London. After independence he led the committee that wrote India's Constitution, adopted in 1950. It banned untouchability and made room for the policy known as *reservations*.

Reservations set aside a share of seats in public colleges, government jobs and legislatures. At first they covered *Scheduled Castes*, the official name for groups once treated as untouchable, and Scheduled Tribes. In 1990 the government extended reservations to groups called Other Backward Classes, following the Mandal Commission report. In 1992 India's Supreme Court ruled that reservations should generally not go above 50 percent.

Supporters say reservations have opened doors for millions. They point to Dalit doctors, officers and members of Parliament whose families were once shut out. Dalit, meaning broken or oppressed, is a name many members of these communities chose for themselves. Supporters say caste bias still exists, so the help is still needed.

Critics raise other points. Some say benefits go mostly to better-off families within each group. Others argue that jobs should go by merit or by family income, not by caste. In 2019 India added a 10 percent reservation for poorer families outside the older groups. The debate continues in courts, colleges and elections.

words.d: India's policy of setting aside seats in colleges, jobs and legislatures for groups that faced discrimination
the official Indian name for caste groups once treated as untouchable
a name meaning broken or oppressed, chosen by many people from communities once treated as untouchable

look.title: Ambedkar on Political and Social Equality
look.text: Ambedkar warned that on January 26, 1950, India would enter a life of contradictions. In politics each person would have one vote and one value. But in social and economic life, deep inequality would remain. He argued that the country must remove this contradiction soon, or those who suffered from inequality would lose faith in democracy.
look.cite: B. R. Ambedkar, speech to the Constituent Assembly of India, November 25, 1949 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What is the contradiction Ambedkar describes? How might reservations be one attempt to address it?

check.q: Who led the committee that wrote India's Constitution?
check.why: Ambedkar, born into a caste treated as untouchable, led the drafting committee for the 1950 Constitution.

check.q: What did India's Supreme Court rule in 1992 about reservations?
choices: They should generally not go above 50 percent
They apply only to private companies
They must cover 90 percent of seats
check.why: The reading says the 1992 ruling set a general limit of 50 percent.

check.q: What is one criticism of reservations named in the reading?
choices: They were never written into law
Benefits may go mostly to better-off families within each group
check.why: Some critics say the better-off families within reserved groups gain most of the benefits.

lessons.title: China's Great Climb
lessons.mainIdea: After reforms began in 1978, China's economy grew fast and hundreds of millions of people left extreme poverty, while new gaps also opened.
reading: In 1978, most people in China were farmers, and most were very poor. That year, a group of farmers in the village of Xiaogang secretly divided their collective land. Each family agreed to farm its own plot and keep what it grew above a quota. Their harvest jumped. Soon the government under Deng Xiaoping allowed this system across the country.

These changes were called *reform and opening*. Farmers could sell extra crops at market prices. In 1980 China created *special economic zones*, such as Shenzhen, where foreign companies could build factories. Shenzhen grew from a small town into one of the world's great cities. The Communist Party kept political control, but the economy became much more open to markets.

The results were huge. The World Bank estimates that close to 800 million people in China left extreme poverty from 1978 to about 2020. That is roughly three-quarters of the global drop in extreme poverty over those years. Millions moved from villages to cities to work in factories, building roads and shipping goods around the world.

The climb also brought new gaps. China's Gini rose, and coastal cities pulled ahead of inland villages. The *hukou* system, a household registration rule, often kept migrant workers from getting the same schools and health care as city-born residents. Some credit markets for the growth. Others credit the state's planning. Both sides study China closely.

words.d: China's economic changes after 1978 that allowed markets, private farming and foreign investment
an area with special rules to attract foreign companies and trade, such as Shenzhen
China's household registration system, which ties people's public services to their hometown

look.title: Two Readings of China's Growth
look.text: Economist A: China grew once it let farmers sell crops and let businesses compete. Markets and trade did the heavy lifting. Economist B: China grew because a strong state built roads, ports and power plants, and chose which industries to support. Markets alone would not have done it.
look.prompt: What evidence from the reading could each economist use? Which facts fit both views?

check.q: What did the farmers of Xiaogang do in 1978?
choices: They built a factory for foreign companies
They secretly divided collective land into family plots
check.why: The farmers divided their collective land so each family farmed its own plot, and harvests rose.

check.q: About how many people in China left extreme poverty from 1978 to about 2020, according to the World Bank?
check.why: The World Bank estimates close to 800 million people left extreme poverty in China over those years.

check.q: How did the hukou system create a gap?
choices: It often kept migrant workers from equal city schools and health care
It gave all land to foreign companies
check.why: Hukou ties services to a person's registered hometown, so many migrants in cities had fewer public services.

lessons.title: Explanations From Left and Right
lessons.mainIdea: People on the left and right often explain inequality differently, and each side points to real evidence.
reading: Two students watch the same news story about a closed factory in a small town. One says the company and the government let those workers down. The other says the town needs new businesses and workers need new skills. Both care about the workers. They just start from different ideas about what causes gaps and what fixes them.

Thinkers on the political *left* often stress *structural* causes. These are forces bigger than one person, such as unequal schools, discrimination, weak unions or tax rules that favor the rich. The philosopher John Rawls argued in 1971 that a fair society allows inequalities only if they help the worst-off. The left often supports higher taxes on the rich, stronger unions and public programs.

Thinkers on the political *right* often stress freedom, markets and personal responsibility. They argue that growth lifts most people, even if some rise faster. They point out that high taxes can weaken the reasons to work, save and invent. The economist Milton Friedman argued that putting equality ahead of freedom would harm both. The right often supports lower taxes, school choice and strong families.

Many people mix these views. Most agree that both personal choices and outside forces shape lives. The debate is about how much weight each deserves, and what a government should do. Good arguments on either side use evidence, like the data in this chapter.

words.d: caused by the way a whole society is set up, rather than by one person's choices
the side of politics that usually stresses equality and a larger role for government in reducing gaps
the side of politics that usually stresses freedom, markets, tradition and personal responsibility

look.title: Friedman on Equality and Freedom
look.text: Friedman argued that a society that puts equality of outcome ahead of freedom will end up with neither. A society that puts freedom first, he said, will end up with a great deal of both freedom and equality.
look.cite: Milton and Rose Friedman, Free to Choose, 1980 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Explain Friedman's claim in your own words. How might a follower of John Rawls answer him?

check.q: Which explanation of inequality is most typical of the political left?
choices: Growth lifts everyone, so gaps do not matter
Structural causes like unequal schools and weak unions
High taxes are the main cause of poverty
Personal choices are the only cause
check.why: The reading says the left often stresses structural causes that are bigger than one person.

check.q: What did John Rawls argue in 1971?
choices: Inequality is fair only if it helps the worst-off
check.why: Rawls argued that a fair society allows inequalities only when they benefit the worst-off.

check.q: What does the reading say most people actually do?
choices: Mix views, agreeing that choices and outside forces both matter
check.why: The reading says many people mix views and argue about how much weight each cause deserves.

lessons.title: Tools Countries Use
lessons.mainIdea: Countries use taxes, public services and growth policies to shape inequality and mobility, and each tool has supporters and critics.
reading: Norway taxes its citizens heavily and pays for free college, long paid parental leave and public health care. Singapore keeps many taxes low but requires workers to save part of every paycheck and builds public housing where most citizens live. Both countries are rich. They took different paths to share the gains.

One common tool is *redistribution*, moving money from richer to poorer through taxes and benefits. A *progressive tax* takes a higher percentage from higher incomes. In many European countries, taxes and benefits cut the Gini a great deal compared with income before taxes. Supporters say this protects families and gives children a fairer start. Critics say high taxes can slow growth and reduce the reward for effort.

Other tools focus on opportunity rather than outcomes. These include early childhood programs, job training and scholarships. Some focus on growth, such as lowering barriers to starting a business. Supporters on the right often argue that a growing economy creates more jobs and more chances to climb.

No country uses only one tool. Most mix taxes, public services and markets in different amounts. Voters in each country argue about the right mix. The best choice depends on what people value most, such as equality, freedom, security or growth, and on what the evidence shows works.

words.d: moving money from richer to poorer people through taxes and government benefits
a tax that takes a higher percentage from people with higher incomes
services paid for by government, such as schools, roads and health care

look.title: Design a Policy
look.text: Your town council has money for one new program. Option 1: free preschool for every four-year-old. Option 2: a tax cut for small businesses that hire local workers. Option 3: a cash payment to the lowest-income families each month.
look.prompt: Pick one option. Explain whether it mainly targets outcomes, opportunity or growth, and give one argument a critic might make.

check.q: What is a progressive tax?
choices: A tax everyone pays at the same rate
A tax that rises every year
A tax that takes a higher percentage from higher incomes
check.why: A progressive tax takes a larger share of income from people who earn more.

check.q: How does Singapore's approach differ from Norway's in the reading?
choices: Singapore keeps many taxes low but requires savings and builds public housing
Singapore taxes more heavily than Norway
Singapore has free college for all
check.why: The reading contrasts Norway's heavy taxes and services with Singapore's low taxes, required savings and public housing.

check.q: Which tool focuses on opportunity rather than outcomes?
check.why: The reading lists early childhood programs, training and scholarships as tools aimed at opportunity.

review.q: A retired teacher owns a paid-off home but lives on a small pension. She has:
review.why: Her pension is a small income, but her paid-off home is wealth.

review.q: Which country would most likely have the lowest Gini coefficient?
review.why: Nordic countries like Norway score in the mid to high 20s, among the most equal in the world.

review.q: What does the Great Gatsby curve show?
choices: Richer countries always have more mobility
More unequal countries tend to have less mobility between generations
review.why: The curve is a correlation: higher inequality tends to go with higher earnings persistence.

review.q: How are India's reservations and Britain's debate about private schools alike?
choices: Both are about who gets access to top schools and jobs
Both were created by the World Bank
review.why: Both debates ask whether the paths to top schools and jobs are open fairly to all groups.

review.q: What began in China in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping?
review.why: China's reform and opening allowed family farming, markets and later special economic zones.

review.q: Which measure would call a family poor for earning far below the middle income in its own country?
review.why: Relative poverty compares a family with others in the same country.

review.q: A speaker says, "Unequal schools and weak unions hold people back." Which view is this closest to?
choices: A structural view often held on the left
A view that only markets matter
A view held only by the World Bank
review.why: Stressing forces bigger than one person, like schools and unions, is a structural view often linked with the left.
